source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do NC crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning?
finding: Three of six crows solved a two-trap tube, kept avoiding the trap when arbitrary cues were removed, failed when a hole and a functional trap were both present, then solved the visually different trap-table.
numbers: 3 of 6 crows solved initial trap-tube; the 3 passed all 4 transfers (abstract only read; full text blocked).
quote: These crows continued to avoid the trap when the arbitrary features that had previously been associated with successful performances were removed.
limits: Abstract only; full paper text was not retrievable this session. Small n (3 successful birds).
agent_relevance: G3: a pass counts only when it survives removal of the cues the agent was fitted on.

source: Taylor (2020) Folk Physics for Crows? Animal Behavior and Cognition 7(3)
finding: Taylor himself now reads the 2009 result as causal understanding of observable features only. The crows failed the two-hole transfer where only one hole had a base, so they treated the meat-hole relation as the cue, not gravity.
numbers: Of 6 crows, 3 learned the trap-tube then passed cue-removal, inverted-tube control and trap-table. All failed the two-hole (one with base) transfer.
quote: the crows had knowledge of the meat's relation with the hole as a proximate causal regularity but did not infer the existence of a distal causal mechanism (gravity).
limits: Interpretation by the original lead author; a review, not new data.
agent_relevance: The best discriminating test is a variant where the surface rule and the deep rule give different answers. Build G3 holdouts that way.

source: Taylor (2020) Folk Physics for Crows? - weight-inattention follow-up
finding: Crows dropping stones on a platform seem to follow a contact rule, not a force rule. Neilands et al. (2016) found no preference for heavy over light objects of different colours.
numbers: No crow showed a preference for heavy over light objects in the Neilands 2016 test (per Taylor 2020 summary).
limits: Second-hand summary; the primary Neilands paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: A correct answer can hide a wrong rule. Test a case where the wrong rule predicts a specific error.

source: Taylor (2020) Folk Physics for Crows? - design critique
finding: Taylor argues the tests jump in difficulty: from using observable cues to inferring unobservable mechanisms. A fairer design ratchets up from hidden objects to hidden agents to unobservable mechanisms in the same paradigm.
numbers: Cites performance swings across task versions: push versus rake (Mulcahy and Call 2006), string tasks, wind-weight task (Jelbert 2019), metatool preplanning (Gruber 2019).
limits: Argues for caution: failure may reflect task design, not missing ability.
agent_relevance: A failed transfer probe can mean a hard probe. Use graded probes with baselines before concluding the agent lacks a skill.

source: Martin-Ordas, Call, Colmenares (2008) Tubes, tables and traps
finding: Great apes solved both trap-tube and trap-platform but performance on the two was uncorrelated. No evidence of transfer across the two functionally equivalent tasks.
numbers: N=20 apes (6 orangutans, 6 chimps, 5 bonobos, 3 gorillas). 12/20 solved platform, 8/20 tube, 5 both, 5 neither. Cross-task r=0.13, p=0.57. First trial not above chance (platform 14/20 p=0.074; tube 12/20 p=0.37).
quote: There was no correlation in the level of performance between the two tasks.
limits: Short tube and tool may have helped. One-tailed tests. Gorillas n=3.
agent_relevance: Success on one framing did not carry to an equivalent framing. Do not assume transfer; measure it.

source: Martin-Ordas et al. (2008) - platform vs tube and prior experience
finding: Platform was easier than tube, performance improved over sessions, and earlier trap experience did not help.
numbers: Platform vs tube F(1,16)=3.46, p=0.04 one-tailed. Session effect F(2,16)=5.99, p=0.006. Prior experience t(18)=0.35, p=0.37. Raking 64.5% vs pushing 18% in the pretest.
limits: Marginal one-tailed effects. 36 trials per task.
agent_relevance: Repeated exposure raised success without showing understanding. Learning curves alone cannot separate cue learning from causal grasp.

source: Logan, Jelbert, Breen, Gray, Taylor (2014) Modifications to the Aesop's Fable paradigm change NC crow performances
finding: Crows prefer water to sand and sinking or solid objects to floating or hollow ones. The first U-tube success was cue learning: all crows then failed the U-tube with the connection exposed.
numbers: 6 crows tested. One crow (Kitty) solved the colour-cued U-tube, then all failed the exposed-connection U-tube. 3 of 6 chose the narrow tube with equal water, then switched to wide when wide had more water.
quote: Kitty's success on the colored U-tube was due to the color cue association and not to the inference of a hidden causal mechanism.
limits: Small n. Fixed task order. Preference for narrow tubes may follow other cues.
agent_relevance: Same shape as trap-tube: success on a cued version, collapse when the cue is removed or the structure changed.

source: Jelbert, Taylor, Cheke, Clayton, Gray (2014) Using the Aesop's Fable paradigm to investigate water displacement by NC crows
finding: Crows chose the functional option in four of six water-displacement tests but failed the narrow versus wide tube and the U-tube. Fast learning, not insight.
numbers: Exp 1 water vs sand: 76.3% to water, binomial p=0.001. Exp 2 sinking: 88.0%. Exp 3 solid: 89.0%. Exp 4 narrow vs wide: 39.3% to narrow, first drop 56% narrow, p=0.27. U-tube: all failed. Birds per experiment: 6, 6, 5, 5, 4, 4.
limits: Fixed order of tasks; 4 of 6 birds finished all. Authors do not generalise the failure to the species.
agent_relevance: Same task family, mixed pass and fail pattern. Report each probe separately instead of one pooled score.

source: Jelbert, Taylor, Gray (2015) Investigating animal cognition with the Aesop's Fable paradigm: current understanding and future directions
finding: Review of Aesop's fable work in rooks, jays, NC crows and children. Two rivals remain unruled out: perceptual-motor feedback (repeat actions that move the reward) and object bias.
numbers: Corvids pass sink/float, solid/hollow, water/sand and water-level tests; jays and crows fail the U-tube.
limits: Review; no new data.
agent_relevance: Pure feedback-driven repeat of what worked can mimic causal understanding. Check that the agent changes behaviour when feedback is withheld.

source: Hennefield, Hwang, Weston, Povinelli (2018) Meta-analytic techniques reveal that corvid causal reasoning in the Aesop's Fable paradigm is driven by trial-and-error learning
finding: Pooled five articles and over 32 experiments. Birds learned from successful drops but not from unsuccessful ones. No transfer across tasks. Authors conclude the paradigm cannot tell trial-and-error from causal reasoning.
numbers: 5 articles, over 32 experiments (abstract). No effect sizes read.
limits: Abstract only. Authors are from a lab with a prior skeptical stance (Povinelli).
agent_relevance: Learning only from success is a mark of reinforcement, not of a causal model. Check whether the agent updates from failures.

source: Ghirlanda and Lind (2017) Aesop's fable experiments demonstrate trial-and-error learning in birds, but no causal understanding
finding: Re-analysis of trial-level data separates initial preference from learning. Found trial-and-error learning in many tasks and initial preference in a few.
numbers: No numbers read (search snippet only).
limits: Not opened. Abstract paraphrase from a search result.
agent_relevance: Look at trial-level learning curves, not final accuracy.

source: Taylor, Roberts, Hunt, Gray (2009) Causal reasoning in NC crows: ruling out spatial analogies and sampling error
finding: A follow-up with eight new stick-tool-experienced crows. Of 14 crows on the trap-table, only the three that solved the trap-tube solved the trap-table.
numbers: 14 crows total on trap-table (8 new plus 6 original); 3 passed. Crows avoided the hole only when functionally placed.
limits: Abstract plus search summary only. Same lab.
agent_relevance: Transfer success tracked prior mastery of the source task, not general bird ability.

source: Tebbich, Seed, Emery, Clayton (2007) Non-tool-using rooks solve the trap-tube problem
finding: Three of seven rooks solved a modified trap-tube but none passed the novel transfer tests. The authors found no evidence of causal understanding.
numbers: 3 of 7 rooks solved; 0 passed transfer (search snippet).
limits: Not opened. Paywalled.
agent_relevance: Tool use is not required to solve the task; solving is not evidence of a model.

source: Mulcahy and Call (2006) How great apes perform on a modified trap-tube task
finding: Apes did better when they could rake the reward toward them than push it away. Success depended on the action allowed.
numbers: 10 apes (5 orangutans, 2 chimps, 2 bonobos, 1 gorilla) per search snippet.
limits: Not opened. Paywalled.
agent_relevance: Same cognition, different action format, different score. Vary the response format as a moderator.

source: Povinelli (2000) Folk physics for apes
finding: Povinelli's reinterpretation hypothesis: apes learn regularities between observable events, not unobservable forces. Chimpanzees showed little understanding of the trap.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: The rival theory that defines what the test must rule out: observable-regularity learning.

source: Taylor (2020) - hidden-agent study and its associative rivals
finding: Taylor 2012 hidden-human study: crows seemed to infer a hidden human caused a stick to move. Rival associative accounts (Boogert 2013; Dymond 2013) were published and answered by the authors.
numbers: No numbers given in the review.
limits: Described second-hand; the study itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Existence of a rival associative account is not proof; check whether it explains all the results.

source: Mecattaf, Slater, Tesic, Prunty, Voudouris, Cheke (2024) A little less conversation, a little more action
finding: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro controlled an agent in Animal-AI tests built from animal experiments. All were outperformed by 59 children and never beat the top 10 competition agents.
numbers: 40 tasks (4 per level, 10 levels), 3 trials each = 12 trials per level per model. LLMs did some of levels 1-2, sporadic on levels 5, 6, 8, near floor elsewhere. 59 children aged 6-10.
quote: LLMs are currently outperformed by human children on these tasks.
limits: Coarse action scripts; few trials per level; floor effects hide differences.
agent_relevance: Embodied tasks drawn from animal labs are a usable LLM benchmark. LLMs fail the harder tool and transfer levels.

source: Mecattaf et al. (2024) - in-context example effect
finding: Giving an expert worked example did not reliably help. Claude got slightly worse on level 1, GPT-4o rose on levels 2-3, Gemini fell on levels 2-3.
numbers: 12 trials per level per model, 3 models, with and without one expert example.
limits: Tiny trial counts, so differences are tentative.
agent_relevance: One worked example is not a dependable fix for physical transfer. Do not count on exemplar prompting for G3.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual tasks
finding: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude and PaLM-2 do above chance on counterfactual variants of 11 tasks but drop sharply versus default versions. This is the LLM version of trap-table transfer.
numbers: 11 tasks; counterfactual performance above random for most but lower than default for all.
quote: these models' ability on these tasks is supported at least in part by nontransferable, default-condition-specific behaviors
limits: Counterfactual worlds are relative; comprehension checks were needed.
agent_relevance: Run the default and a counterfactual of the same structure. The gap shows how much of the pass was recall of the familiar form.

source: Wu et al. (2024) - correlation and model differences
finding: Default and counterfactual accuracy correlate, so ordinary benchmarks still carry signal. Some models show the reverse: best default, worst counterfactual.
numbers: GPT-4 had top default spatial accuracy but the largest counterfactual drop; PaLM-2 was lower by default but most robust.
limits: Training data differences confound the comparison.
agent_relevance: Do not drop ordinary tests; add the counterfactual to them.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: GPT models solved letter-string analogies on the usual alphabet but dropped sharply on permuted or symbol alphabets. Humans stayed level.
numbers: Humans 0.753 (CI 0.734-0.773; 1,876 samples; 136 participants). GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each; all alphabet types pooled).
limits: Comprehension checks were high but not perfect. Older GPT models only.
agent_relevance: An analogy pass on the familiar form is weak evidence. Humans keep accuracy under relabeling, models do not.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) - error types
finding: Models make different errors from humans. Humans often apply a valid alternative rule; GPT models more often apply an incorrect rule.
numbers: Alternate rule: GPT-3 5.81%, GPT-4 22.00%, humans 38.59% of errors. Incorrect rule: 30.97%, 32.67%, 14.67%.
limits: Hand-coded error classes.
agent_relevance: Analyse the kind of wrong answer, not just the wrong rate, to tell cue use from rule use.

source: Schulze Buschoff, Akata, Bethge, Schulz (2024) Visual cognition in multimodal LLMs
finding: Vision LLMs partly solve intuitive-physics and causal tasks but none match humans. GPT-4V and Claude-3 Opus were above chance in two of three domains.
numbers: Jenga task: 42 images, 42 human participants. GPT-4V differs from humans t(42)=2.59, p<.05. Responsibility rating: GPT-4V regression coefficient 0.16 (CI 0.10-0.21, R2=0.027) vs human-to-human 0.54 (R2=0.268). Other models gave constant ratings (100 or 50).
limits: Static images, simple stimuli, few images.
agent_relevance: Constant answers across scenes are a sign of cue-blind responding; check that the agent's answers vary with the scene.

source: Schulze Buschoff et al. (2024) - Michotte launching task
finding: Models struggled to read ball direction even though the prompt said the arrows show it. The counterfactual question was the harder probe.
numbers: 18 images; 14 human subjects in outcome condition, 13 in counterfactual condition (Gerstenberg design).
limits: Static 2D images instead of video.
agent_relevance: Counterfactual judgement is the more diagnostic probe.

source: Schulze Buschoff, Voudouris, Akata, Bethge, Tenenbaum, Schulz (2025) Testing the limits of fine-tuning for visual cognition in VLMs
finding: Fine-tuning vision-language models on tower stability or counterfactual stability raised accuracy in that domain, including taller towers, but did not transfer to the other domain or to real-photo towers.
numbers: Models up to 90B parameters; naturalistic set of 100 real tower images (Lerer 2016); humans averaged 0.72 on pyramids. Fine-tuned on one domain: no gain on the other, even with paired images and the red block named.
quote: task-specific fine-tuning does not contribute to robust human-like generalization to data with other visual characteristics or to tasks in other cognitive domains
limits: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning only; larger models untested.
agent_relevance: Training on a task family gave in-distribution gains but not trap-table-style transfer. A scaffold is likely to face the same limit.

source: Rane et al. (2025) Position: Principles of Animal Cognition to Improve LLM Evaluations
finding: Argues five principles from animal cognition (for example, control for low-level explanations) should guide LLM tests. Case study on transitive inference.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Direct support for building controls like cue removal and inverted configurations into agent checks.
